newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy rejects notion of early 1998 budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy rejects notion of early 1998 budget.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government will not bring forward presentation of the country's 1998 budget, Treasury Ministry sources said on Friday.

They said the bill would be presented to parliament as in past years by September 30. Prime Minister Romano Prodi earlier this year suggested early presentation to generate confidence in Italy's ability to join Europe's planned single currency.

Since the proposal, the government has instead drawn up a supplementary budget of 15.5 trillion lire ($9.4 billion) for 1997 to ensure Italy's public deficit remains inside the target set for countries wanting to qualify for monetary union.
"Bringing forward the 1998 budget can be excluded," one senior Treasury Ministry source said.
The source said the normal timeframe for presentation of the government's rolling three-year economic targets would also be respected. The document, known as the DPEF, has to be drawn up by May 15.
Under Italian law, the annual budget must be presented to parliament by September 30 and be passed into law by both houses by December 31.

This year's mini-budget has drawn criticism from industry and opposition for not addressing structural reforms to state spending and instead raising revenue by making employers pay taxes ahead of schedule on big severance payment funds they hold.
Prodi has said eventual reform to welfare spending, including costly pensions, will be enshrined in the 1998 budget.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Friday that comments on pensions by state auditor Andrea Monorchio did not reflect the government's position on the matter.

Monorchio told a parliamentary commission on Thursday that so-called seniority pensions, which can be drawn after 40 years of contributions have been paid by an employee into a state retirement fund, should be phased out.
He said in future all Italians should expect to retire at the age of 65 and earlier pensions should only be granted in special cases.
Ciampi, asked by reporters whether the Treasury and government shared Monorchio's views, replied:

"(The proposal) is not from the Treasury or the government...there is only one valid line and it is that declared by the Prime Minister...who has announced that he is beginning talks with unions and employers."
Unions have consistently said that the pensions system cannot be touched before 1998, as agreed in a previous pension reform deal worked out in 1995.
